section_insight: Three high-signal findings stand out. First, `TopBar.tsx` ↔ `db.ts` (strength 0.75) is the strongest non-trivial coupling in the codebase: a UI chrome component co-changes with the database layer on 6 of 8 commits. There is no plausible import relationship here — this is a shared assumption about data shape or auth state leaking into presentation. Extract whatever DB concern TopBar is reacting to (likely session/user or nav counts) into a dedicated query hook or server component so the chrome layer stops tracking schema changes. Second, the `whoop/` module cluster (`client.ts` ↔ `token.ts`, `client.ts` ↔ `upsert.ts`, `sync.ts` ↔ `client.ts`, all at 0.67) forms a tight co-change group that spans auth, HTTP, and persistence in lockstep. These three files move together because they share assumptions about token shape and refresh behavior that are not encoded anywhere — they live in each file's head. Extract a `WhoopSession` or `WhoopConfig` struct (token, expiry, userId) passed explicitly, so a token-format change touches one definition instead of rippling across all three. Third, `apps/web/src/lib/db/sleep.ts` ↔ `streamlit/whoop/db.py` (strength 0.57) is the sharpest cross-package signal: a TypeScript DB module and a Python Streamlit query file move in sync across 4 commits. They are duplicating the same schema knowledge in two languages with no shared source of truth. Define the sleep record schema once — either as a SQL migration or a shared JSON schema — and have both consumers derive from it. The `db/connection.ts` file (24 commits, coupled to nearly every module at 0.12–0.37) is a hub rather than a coupling problem, but its breadth confirms it is doing too much: schema initialization, connection pooling, and possibly migration logic are all mixed in one place, which is why everything touches it during any structural change.
